'''Anthony Frederick Orchard''' (13 March 1941 – 19 August 2005) was a Welsh [[Inorganic chemistry|inorganic chemist]].<ref name="independent">{{cite news| url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/a-f-orchard-321363.html | department=Obituaries | title=A. F. Orchard: Gifted research chemist and teacher | newspaper=[[The Independent]] | date= 22 October 2005 }}</ref><ref name="cherwell">{{cite news| url=http://www.cherwell.org/news/2005/10/05/leading-chemist-dies | department=News | title=Leading chemist dies | first=Huan | last=Zhao | newspaper=[[Cherwell (newspaper)|Cherwell]] | date= 5 October 2005 }}</ref> His research contributed to laying the foundations of much modern consumer [[electronic technology]].<ref name="guardian">{{cite news| url=https://www.theguardian.com/news/2005/sep/20/guardianobituaries.obituaries | department=Obituary | title=Tony Orchard: Chemist who made today's consumer electronics possible | first=Tom | last=Kelly | newspaper=[[The Guardian]] | date= 20 September 2005 }}</ref>

Tony Orchard was born in [[Carmarthen]], [[Wales]], and moved to [[Swansea]]. He studied [[Chemistry]] first at [[Wadham College, Oxford]] as an undergraduate and then towards a [[DPhil]] doctoral degree in [[Theoretical chemistry|theoretical]] [[inorganic chemistry]] at [[Merton College, Oxford]]. He left Merton College before he had completed his doctorate at the age of 26 to become a [[Fellow (college)|Fellow]] in Inorganic Chemistry at [[University College, Oxford|University College]] in [[Oxford]].<ref name="chem-oxford">{{cite book| editor-first1=Robert J. P. | editor-last1=Williams | editor-first2=Allan | editor-last2=Chapman | editor-link2=Allan Chapman (historian) | editor-first3=John S. | editor-last3=Rowlinson | title=Chemistry at Oxford: A History from 1600 to 2005 | url=https://archive.org/details/chemistryatoxfor2005will | url-access=limited | publisher=[[RSC Publishing]] | location=UK | year=2009 | isbn=978-0-85404-139-8 | pages=[https://archive.org/details/chemistryatoxfor2005will/page/n259 250], 255, 265, 272 }}</ref> He stayed at University College until his death.

During the 1970s, Orchard led a group of researchers working in the area of [[photoelectron spectroscopy]]. This enabled scientists to examine the [[electronic structure]] of materials. The research was important for technological innovations in modern [[electronics]], helping with the development of advances such as the [[personal computer]] and [[mobile phone]]. He published the book ''Magnetochemistry'' in 2003.<ref>{{cite book| title=Magnetochemistry | year=2003 | publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] | location=Oxford | url=http://www.abebooks.co.uk/9780198792789/Magnetochemistry-Orchard-Tony-A-F-0198792786/plp | isbn=978-0198792789 }}</ref>

In addition to his research contributions,, Orchard also helped to improve the system of undergraduate applications for chemistry at [[Oxford University]].<ref name="cherwell" />

==Personal life==
Tony Orchard was an amateur sportsman, playing [[tennis]] and [[snooker]].<ref name="cherwell" /> At an early age, he won snooker games with the later world champions [[Terry Griffiths]] and [[Ray Reardon]]. Orchard's friends included former [[United States]] president [[Bill Clinton]], who he met during the 1960s when Clinton was studying at University College as a [[Rhodes Scholar]]. Orchard was married to his wife Jeanne and later divorced, with two sons and two daughters. He died aged 64 of [[colon cancer]].{{Citation needed|date=June 2026}}
